title: Pictures, Storyboards, and Visual Standards
subtitle: Some things are far easier to show than to say. A written standard tells you what to do; a visual standard shows you what right looks like. This chapter adds the last kind of standard, the one a picture carries better than any list: a photo of the ideal state, and a short storyboard of the steps. With it, the fifth S is complete.
part_position: Third and FINAL chapter of Part Seven (Standardize); it COMPLETES Standardize, the fifth of the six S's, by adding the last kind of standard, the one a picture carries better than words. It follows Chapter 24 (Checklists, Schedules, and Responsibilities), which gave standards their three tools, and hands off to Chapter 26 (Sustain: Keeping the Gains), which opens Part Eight, the sixth and final S. Four of the six S's were complete going in (Sort, Straighten, Shine, Safety); after this chapter FIVE of six are done and only Sustain remains
opens_part: None; Chapter 23 opened Part Seven (Standardize) with the concept of a standard. Chapter 25 is the THIRD and FINAL chapter of Part Seven
completes_part: Part Seven (Standardize); Chapter 25 adds the last kind of standard, the visual standard, and COMPLETES the fifth S at the STANDARDIZE COMPLETE milestone. Sustain (Chapters 26 to 30) opens next and is the sixth and final S
hands_off_note: Chapter 25 COMPLETES Standardize, the fifth S. Chapter 23 gave the CONCEPT of a standard (the best way you know today, written down) and Chapter 24 gave standards the three TOOLS that make them run (a checklist for the what, a schedule for the when, a name for the who); both HELD the friction meter and built, then reinforced, a catch behind the needle that keeps a gain from sliding back. For most recurring work, words and tools are enough, but there is an edge where words strain: try to write down exactly what a tidy shelf looks like, how the cables coil, or where each thing sits when the room is right, and you pile up clauses that still miss it. Some things simply resist description; the problem is not the people and not the standard but the medium. Chapter 25 adds the last kind of standard, the one words handle poorly: the VISUAL standard, the standard you show instead of tell. It delivers the show-do-not-tell reframe and the definition box (a written standard tells you what to do, a visual standard shows you what right looks like). It delivers the flagship, the PHOTO OF THE IDEAL STATE (photograph a space when it is exactly right and that photo becomes the standard anyone can match reality against at a glance; the optimistic mirror image of the before photo from Prepare, posted where the space is). It delivers the STORYBOARD (for a task with steps, a short strip of pictures beats a paragraph, the few frames that matter in order, so the next person copies what they see). It delivers the craft of making a visual standard MATCH-ABLE (shoot from the angle and in the light of use, put it where the work happens at the point of use, keep it honest rather than laminated, because a visual standard filed away is a contradiction in terms). Because this COMPLETES the fifth S, the friction meter reaches a marked STANDARDIZE COMPLETE MILESTONE, the fifth on the dial after Sort, Straighten, Shine, and Safety; the needle takes a small, honest tick forward and the anti-backslide catch behind it is drawn FULLY ENGAGED and LOCKED, its firmest state yet. The tick is deliberately tiny because Standardize secured what was already built rather than clearing new ground; the real change is the catch, not the needle. This IS a MILESTONE (the fifth), with the anti-backslide catch fully engaged. FIVE of the six S's are done. The GOAL crosshair, tagged purpose, is a step away on the green calm side, because one S remains, Sustain, which keeps a held home held over the years. Chapter 26 (Sustain: Keeping the Gains) opens Part Eight and the sixth and final S.
audience: Readers who have finished four of the six S's and, across Chapters 23 and 24, grasped the concept of a standard (the best way you know today, written down) and given standards their three tools (a checklist, a schedule, a name), then hit the edge where words strain. Busy home keepers and parents. They are tired of arguing about what tidy means and of writing careful instructions everyone reads slightly differently, and they sense, correctly, that some things are far easier to show than to say. They do not need Sort, Straighten, Shine, or Safety re-taught, nor the concept of a standard or the three tools re-derived, nor the visual controls that make a storage spot self-explaining (Chapter 14, labels, outlines, boundaries, the Glance Test); they need the last kind of standard, the one a picture carries. A home whose standards live only in words, or only in one person's head, is the normal case, not a failing; a visual standard is a kindness that ends arguments, not a control imposed on the family.
core_promise: Add the last kind of standard and complete the fifth S. See where written standards run out and why some things are far easier to show than to say: the problem is not the people and not the standard but the medium. Make an ideal-state photo, photograph a space when it is exactly right and that photo becomes the standard anyone can match reality against at a glance, posted where the space is. Build a simple storyboard, a short strip of pictures for a task's steps that the next person copies frame by frame. Shoot a visual standard so it is genuinely easy to match, from the angle and in the light of use, and put it at the point of use, honest rather than laminated. Some things are easier to show than to say, so when a picture carries the standard better than words can, the picture is the standard, and with it the fifth S is complete and the home runs on what you have made visible.
emotional_purpose: Deliver warmth, relief, and, as a Part close, quiet pride, never corporate obligation. The danger word for this chapter, as for Chapters 23 and 24, is 'corporate': visual standards can sound like factory signage and management dashboards, so the whole chapter works to keep them human and homely, a photo on the cupboard door, a child's picture of the tidy shelf, never institutional. No shame: a home whose standards live only in words, or only in one person's head, is the normal case; a picture is a kindness that ends arguments, not a control imposed on the family. The ideal-state photo lowers the bar so far that a child too young to read the word tidy can match a shelf to a photo, and letting the children take the photos makes the standard theirs. No force or control metaphors (no enforce, compliance, audit in the punitive sense, lock down), no hype words (unlock, leverage, elevate, seamless, game-changing, single source of truth), no brand names (no named cameras, apps, or label products). Deliver the honest milestone: because Standardize secured what was built rather than clearing new ground, the needle takes only a small, honest tick forward, and the real change is the anti-backslide catch fully engaged and locked, so the home is held against the slide back about as firmly as it can be. The needle barely moved, and the grip behind it is complete, which is exactly what finishing this S was supposed to feel like. Five of six S's are done, and the goal is a step away, because one S remains, Sustain.
practical_purpose: Show where written standards run out and why some things are far easier to show than to say, naming the real cause as the medium (everyone reads the same sentences and rebuilds a slightly different picture, so a shared photo, not better writing, closes the gap). Deliver the hero, the VISUAL standard, in two forms: the PHOTO OF THE IDEAL STATE (photograph a space when it is exactly right and that photo becomes the standard anyone can match reality against at a glance; get the space right on a rare day, take the photo before it drifts, and post it where the space is; the optimistic mirror image of the before photo, this is what it looks like at its best); and the STORYBOARD (for a task with steps, a short strip of a few frames in order beats a numbered paragraph, because the reader copies what they see instead of converting words into actions; four phone snaps or stick-figure sketches are plenty, the value is in the sequence being visible, not the pictures being beautiful). Give the craft of making a visual standard MATCH-ABLE: shoot from the angle and in the light the person will actually have when they set the space right (a photo from a stepladder when everyone sees the pantry from standing height is subtly hard to match, and subtly hard to match means quietly abandoned); put the standard where the work happens, at the point of use, because a visual standard filed away is a contradiction in terms; and keep it honest rather than impressive, a few slightly imperfect photos taped where they are needed beating a beautiful laminated binder in a drawer. hero_device: The visual standard, the standard you show instead of tell, delivered in two forms. The photo of the ideal state: photograph a space when it is exactly right, and that photo becomes the standard, not a description of the ideal state but a picture of it, that anyone can match their reality against at a glance, posted where the space is. The storyboard: for a task with steps, a short strip of pictures beats a paragraph, the few frames that matter in order, so the next person follows the pictures without reading a word. Where a written standard tells you what to do, a visual standard shows you what right looks like, and for anything you would struggle to put into words, the picture is the better standard

worked_example.space: Two ordinary home cases that show the visual standard in each of its forms. First, a shelf or space that should look a certain way (the pantry, the coat closet, the play shelf, the desk): get it exactly right on one of those rare days, and before it drifts take a photograph, then tape it inside the cupboard door or stick it to the wall beside the shelf, so the standard for that space is not in anyone's head or in any document but on the door, and the room either matches the picture or it does not. Second, a task with steps (the entryway reset, setting up and stowing the folding table, coiling the cables and clipping them, sorting the recycling on collection night): make a storyboard, three or four simple frames each showing one key step in order (for the entryway reset: shoes on the rack, bags on the hooks, surface clear), each frame a small photo or stick-figure sketch with a two or three word caption, so the next person copies what they see frame by frame instead of decoding a paragraph. In both cases the craft is the same: shoot from the angle and in the light of use, post it at the point of use, keep it honest rather than laminated.

the_edge_and_the_standard.when_words_are_not_enough: The edge. There is a particular kind of standard that fails not because it is wrong but because it is written: everyone reads the same careful sentences and pictures something slightly different, and slightly different, multiplied across a household, is how a shelf meant to be uniform ends up looking like four people's separate guesses. The problem is not the people and not the standard. It is the medium. This is why tidy causes so many household arguments: it is a word, and words about how things should look are almost infinitely arguable, because we are trying to transmit an image through the narrow pipe of language and each person rebuilds it a little differently at the other end. The moment you stop describing the image and simply show it, the argument evaporates. There is nothing left to interpret; you are both looking at the same photograph and comparing the shelf to it. The show-do-not-tell reframe, frozen: a written standard tells you what to do, a visual standard shows you what right looks like, for anything you would struggle to put into words, that is the difference between a standard people argue about and one they can simply see and match. The definition box, frozen: a visual standard is the ideal state of a space or a task, captured as a picture rather than described in words, a photo of what done looks like, or a short storyboard of the steps, where a written standard tells you what to do, a visual standard shows you what right looks like.
the_edge_and_the_standard.the_photo_of_the_ideal_state: The flagship (the picture of the ideal state). The pictures line, frozen: photograph a space when it is exactly right, and that photo becomes the standard, not a description of the ideal state, but a picture of it, that anyone can match their reality against at a glance. You get a space exactly the way it should be on one of those rare days, and before it drifts you take a photograph, then put it where the space is, taped inside the cupboard door or stuck to the wall beside the shelf, so the standard is not in anyone's head or in any document; it is on the door. You did a version of this at the very start, the before photo, the visual baseline, the honest record of the mess; the ideal-state photo is its optimistic mirror image, not this is what it looked like at its worst but this is what it looks like at its best, and this is what we are keeping it like. A child too young to read the word tidy can match a shelf to a photo. The photo-of-the-ideal-state reframe, frozen: the most powerful standard in a home is often a single photograph, the shelf, the counter, the entryway, captured on the day it was exactly right, from then on, tidy is not an opinion and not an argument, it is a picture on the cupboard door, and the room either matches it or it does not.
the_edge_and_the_standard.the_storyboard: The sequence (the storyboard). A photo of the ideal state is perfect for a space that should look a certain way, but some standards are about a sequence, the steps of a task done in the right order, and for those one photo is not enough, and the answer is not a paragraph but a few pictures. The storyboard line, frozen: for a task with steps, a short strip of pictures beats a paragraph, show the few frames that matter, in order, and the next person can follow the pictures without reading a word. Borrowed without ceremony from the way films are planned, a storyboard is a short strip of simple frames, each showing one key step, laid out in order (how the folding table gets set up and stowed, how the cables coil and where they clip, how the recycling gets sorted on collection night). Three or four little pictures carry more, and faster, than a numbered list, because the reader is not converting words into actions but copying what they see, frame by frame. You do not need to be a photographer or an artist; four phone snaps of your own hands, or four quick stick-figure sketches, are plenty, and the value is entirely in the sequence being visible, not in the pictures being beautiful.
the_edge_and_the_standard.make_it_match_able: The craft (make it match-able). A visual standard only works if it is genuinely easy to match. Shoot the picture from the angle and in the light the person will actually have when they set the space right; a photo of the pantry taken from a stepladder, when everyone else sees it from standing height, is subtly hard to match, and subtly hard to match means quietly abandoned. Get to the real eye line, use the ordinary light of the room, and capture the space the way it is actually seen. Then put the standard where the work happens, not in a folder somewhere sensible, because a visual standard filed away is a contradiction in terms, its entire value being seen at the point of use. And keep it honest rather than impressive: a few slightly imperfect photos taped where they are needed will do more for your home than a beautiful laminated binder that lives in a drawer and helps no one.
the_edge_and_the_standard.the_rule: The rule, frozen (hero): some things are easier to show than to say, when a picture carries the standard better than words can, the picture is the standard. The One Idea to Keep, frozen: when words fall short, show the result instead, photograph a space at its best, or storyboard a task's steps, and put the picture where the work happens, right stops being an argument and becomes something anyone can see and match.

definition: A visual standard is the ideal state of a space or a task, captured as a picture rather than described in words: a photo of what "done" looks like, or a short storyboard of the steps. Where a written standard tells you what to do, a visual standard shows you what right looks like.
rule: Some things are easier to show than to say. When a picture carries the standard better than words can, the picture is the standard.
pictures_line: Photograph a space when it is exactly right, and that photo becomes the standard: not a description of the ideal state, but a picture of it, that anyone can match their reality against at a glance.
storyboard_line: For a task with steps, a short strip of pictures beats a paragraph. Show the few frames that matter, in order, and the next person can follow the pictures without reading a word.
show_do_not_tell_reframe: A written standard tells you what to do. A visual standard shows you what right looks like. For anything you would struggle to put into words, that is the difference between a standard people argue about and one they can simply see and match.
photo_of_the_ideal_state_reframe: The most powerful standard in a home is often a single photograph: the shelf, the counter, the entryway, captured on the day it was exactly right. From then on, tidy is not an opinion and not an argument. It is a picture on the cupboard door, and the room either matches it or it does not.
completion_reframe: With this, the fifth S is complete. The best way you know is written down, carried by a checklist and a schedule and a name, and, where words fall short, shown in a picture. Your home no longer runs on your memory. It runs on what you have made visible.

callouts.quick_win: Photograph one space when it is exactly the way you want it, print it small, and tape it up where the space is. Now "put it back the way it should be" is not an instruction anyone has to remember or interpret. It is a picture to match.
callouts.family_challenge: Let the children take the ideal-state photos and put them up at their own height. A child who took the picture of the tidy shelf is far more likely to put that shelf back the way the picture shows, because the standard is theirs.
callouts.sixs_tip: Shoot the standard photo from the exact angle and in the same light someone will see the space from when they go to set it right. A picture shot from an odd angle or in different light is hard to match, and a standard that is hard to match is one people quietly stop using.
callouts.common_mistake: Building an elaborate laminated binder of visual standards that looks impressive and helps no one, instead of a few honest photos stuck where the work happens. The whole value of a visual standard is being seen at the point of use; a beautiful one filed away is worth nothing.

one_idea_to_keep: When words fall short, show the result instead. Photograph a space at its best, or storyboard a task's steps, and put the picture where the work happens. Right stops being an argument and becomes something anyone can see and match.
